newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rumblings in Thai government over Amnuay's future.
newsitem.headline: Rumblings in Thai government over Amnuay's future.

text.p: Coalition partners in the Thai government are making a fresh push for the removal of embattled Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, who is frantically trying to put the nation's woeful economy back on track.

The sharpening of knives against Amnuay comes at a pivotal time as the nation's once-buoyant economy sputters, troubles are rife in the depressed finance and property sectors, the baht is threatened with speculative attacks and the stock market languishes at eight-year lows.

Political sources told Reuters on Monday some members of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's six-party coalition government were jostling for a cabinet reshuffle with demands for the unelected Amnuay's removal.
Last month, when the baht came under speculative attack, Amnuay and Chavalit were forced to deny rumours that the finance minister would be removed.

Economic and political analysts said the pressure for Amnuay's removal had resurfaced at a delicate time as foreign investor confidence in Thailand was low and there was no heir apparent to Amnuay, who they said has done a reasonably good job so far.
Chavalit came to power last December and handpicked Amnuay to put the already stumbling economy back on track.
But Amnuay's sweeping economic revival measures, sometimes introduced without consultation with other senior politicians, ruffled some feathers, political sources said.

Some senior members of Chavalit's own New Aspiration Party (NAP) were seeking Amnuay's removal with assistance from others in the second biggest coalition partner, the Chart Pattana Party (CPP), which has made no secret of its desire to hold key economic portfolios in government, they added.

"The prime minister had promised a cabinet reshuffle after his government ruled for six months. Its six months now and people are pressing him on his promise and Amnuay is the target of change," said an NAP source.
CPP leader Chatichai Choonhavan also said over the weekend after meeting senior NAP officials there would soon be news of a cabinet reshuffle. Chavalit has not commented on the issue.

"Given the underlying mess in the economy, sooner or later some heads will have to roll," said the head of a foreign brokerage who decline to be named. "There have been rumours Amnuay will go and he stands the risk of losing his job. But the question is when."

"There are some in the CPP and NAP who are playing a power game and Chavalit will have to protect himself and there could well be sacrifical lambs, but choices for finance minister are limited...so who?," he added.

Chaiwat Khamchoo, a political scientist from Chulalongkorn University said: "If anybody wants Amnuay out then you must have somebody else who is more capable than him and the choices are limited. I think he won't be removed now."
"If Amnuay is removed it would send a confusing signal to many people, including foreign investors, who are watching the Thai economy closely," he added.
"Major economic problems like the ones Thailand has cannot be solved overnight and it takes time. I don't think anyone in the coalition is more capable than Amnuay," he said.

Analysts said the opposition had so far been lukewarm in its castigation of the government's attempts to bring order to the economy because it was not in a position itself to remedy economic problems quickly if it were to topple the coalition.
"The opposition I think, are not keen on becoming the government now because it is a hot seat," said Chaiwat.

But main opposition Democrat Party spokesman Abhisit Vejjajiva said opposition members were planning a vote of no-confidence in the government over its handling of the economy when parliament resumes session in July.
"We are now discussing the priorities of no-confidence matters ranging from mismanagement of economic policy to poor performance to corruption among some ministers," he added.
